claim: Distal mesenchyme cells from late stage chick wing buds complete proliferative outgrowth by an intrinsic cell cycle timer when grafted to younger wing buds
source: RNA sequencing reveals that distal mesenchyme cells complete proliferative outgrowth by an intrinsic cell cycle timer in the presence of e-m signalling.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by RNA-seq data and grafting experiments

claim: Epithelial-mesenchyme signalling is required permissively to allow the intrinsic cell cycle timer to run its course
source: In this process, e-m signalling is required permissively to allow the intrinsic cell cycle timer to run its course.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing grafted cells respond to FGF signaling

claim: A temporal switch from BMP antagonism to BMP signalling controls the intrinsic cell cycle timer during limb outgrowth
source: We provide evidence that a temporal switch from BMP antagonism to BMP signalling controls the intrinsic cell cycle timer during limb outgrowth.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by gene expression data and functional experiments with BMP and Noggin

claim: Extrinsic signals and intrinsic timers can operate together in parallel in antero-posterior patterning of the limb
source: Recently, it has become evident that both processes can operate together - either in parallel, such as in antero-posterior patterning of the limb (thumb to little finger) (Harfe et al., 2004; Towers et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work

claim: Extrinsic signals and intrinsic timers can operate together in parallel in dorso-ventral patterning of the neural tube
source: Recently, it has become evident that both processes can operate together - either in parallel, such as in antero-posterior patterning of the limb (thumb to little finger) (Harfe et al., 2004; Towers et al., 2011) and in dorso-ventral patterning of the neural tube (Dessaud et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work

claim: Extrinsic signals and intrinsic timers can operate together sequentially in proximo-distal patterning of the limb
source: Recently, it has become evident that both processes can operate together - either in parallel, such as in antero-posterior patterning of the limb (thumb to little finger) (Harfe et al., 2004; Towers et al., 2011) and in dorso-ventral patterning of the neural tube (Dessaud et al., 2007) - or sequentially, such as in proximo-distal patterning of the limb (shoulder to finger tips) (Cooper et al., 2011; Roselló-Díez et al., 2014; Saiz-Lopez et al., 2015; Saiz-Lopez et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work

claim: During early stages of proximo-distal patterning of the chick wing (stage HH19), signals from the main body of the embryo specify proximal identity (humerus)
source: During early stages of proximo-distal patterning of the chick wing (stage Hamburger Hamilton HH19 – see Materials and methods for embryonic days), signals from the main body of the embryo specify proximal identity (humerus) (Cooper et al., 2011; Mercader et al., 1999; Mercader et al., 2000; Roselló-Díez et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work

claim: Once distal mesenchyme cells of the wing bud are displaced by growth away from proximal signals, there is a switch to an intrinsic timing mechanism that specifies distal identity (elbow to digits)
source: Once distal mesenchyme cells of the wing bud are displaced by growth away from proximal signals, there is a switch to an intrinsic timing mechanism that specifies distal identity (elbow to digits) (Saiz-Lopez et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work

claim: The intrinsic timer involves cells executing a programme of proliferation, expressing regulators of distal position (i.e. Hoxa13) and altering their cell surface properties
source: This intrinsic timer involves cells executing a programme of proliferation, expressing regulators of distal position (i.e. Hoxa13) and altering their cell surface properties, which are considered to encode position along the proximo-distal axis.
evidence: This describes the characteristics of the intrinsic timer mechanism based on previous observations

claim: Distal limb bud mesenchyme cells produce a factor that maintains the overlying apical ectodermal ridge
source: In addition, distal limb bud mesenchyme cells produce a factor that maintains the overlying apical ectodermal ridge (Zwilling and Hansborough, 1956)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work

claim: The apical ectodermal ridge is a thickening of the distal epithelium
source: In addition, distal limb bud mesenchyme cells produce a factor that maintains the overlying apical ectodermal ridge (Zwilling and Hansborough, 1956) - a thickening of the distal epithelium
evidence: This is a definition based on established knowledge

claim: The apical ectodermal ridge is required for bud outgrowth until HH29/30
source: In addition, distal limb bud mesenchyme cells produce a factor that maintains the overlying apical ectodermal ridge (Zwilling and Hansborough, 1956) - a thickening of the distal epithelium, which is required for bud outgrowth until HH29/30 (Saiz-Lopez et al., 2015; Saunders, 1948; Summerbell, 1974).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work

claim: The factor that maintains the apical ectodermal ridge is the Bone Morphogenetic Protein (BMP) antagonist Gremlin1 (Grem1)
source: This factor is the Bone Morphogenetic Protein (BMP) antagonist Gremlin1 (Grem1), which maintains expression of genes encoding Fibroblast Growth Factors (FGFs) in the apical ectodermal ridge until HH27 (Merino et al., 1999; Pizette and Niswander, 1999; Zúñiga et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work

claim: Gremlin1 maintains expression of genes encoding Fibroblast Growth Factors (FGFs) in the apical ectodermal ridge until HH27
source: This factor is the Bone Morphogenetic Protein (BMP) antagonist Gremlin1 (Grem1), which maintains expression of genes encoding Fibroblast Growth Factors (FGFs) in the apical ectodermal ridge until HH27 (Merino et al., 1999; Pizette and Niswander, 1999; Zúñiga et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work

claim: Reciprocal signalling between the apical ectodermal ridge and the underlying mesenchyme is considered to maintain outgrowth, first by repressing apoptosis, and then by permissively maintaining cell proliferation
source: Reciprocal signalling between the apical ectodermal ridge and the underlying mesenchyme is considered to maintain outgrowth, first by repressing apoptosis, and then by permissively maintaining cell proliferation (Dudley et al., 2002; Saiz-Lopez et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work

claim: The breakdown of the epithelial-mesenchyme (e-m signalling) feedback loop at HH27, and the subsequent loss of apical ectodermal ridge signalling, is considered necessary to terminate limb bud outgrowth at the end of the patterning phase
source: Thus, the breakdown of the epithelial-mesenchyme (e-m signalling) feedback loop at HH27, and the subsequent loss of apical ectodermal ridge signalling, is considered necessary to terminate limb bud outgrowth at the end of the patterning phase (Zwilling and Hansborough, 1956; Scherz et al., 2004; Verheyden and Sun, 2008).
evidence: This is the longstanding view supported by citations to previous work

claim: The final distal phalanx is laid down at around HH28 in the chick wing
source: Note that the final distal phalanx is laid down at around HH28 in the chick wing (Saunders, 1948; Summerbell, 1974).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work

claim: Later growth of the limb after the apical ectodermal ridge has regressed is caused by the expansion of osteogenic progenitor cells in the developing long bones
source: Later growth of the limb after the apical ectodermal ridge has regressed is caused by the expansion of osteogenic progenitor cells in the developing long bones.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about limb development

claim: Grafts of HH27 mesenchyme cells expressing Green Fluorescent Protein (GFP) that were made to younger HH20 buds and left to develop for 24 hr until HH24 completed their proliferation programme in the presence of an overlying host apical ectodermal ridge
source: However, we recently showed that grafts of HH27 mesenchyme cells expressing Green Fluorescent Protein (GFP) that were made to younger HH20 buds, and which were left to develop for 24 hr until HH24 (now referred to as HH24 graft or HH24g), completed their proliferation programme in the presence of an overlying host apical ectodermal ridge (Saiz-Lopez et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors

claim: HH24g mesenchyme (distal 150 microns of graft) has a similar cell cycle profile to HH29 mesenchyme (stage of donor limb), rather than contralateral HH24 mesenchyme (stage of host)
source: Thus, HH24g mesenchyme (distal 150 microns of graft) has a similar cell cycle profile to HH29 mesenchyme (stage of donor limb), rather than contralateral HH24 mesenchyme (stage of host – Figure 1a - red lines).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1a

claim: Wing buds that develop with HH27-HH20 grafts produce the three main segments of the wing, but the autopod (digits and wrist) is very stunted due to the reduced growth of the grafted tissue relative to host tissue
source: Although wing buds that develop with these grafts produce the three main segments of the wing, the autopod (digits and wrist) is very stunted due to the reduced growth of the grafted tissue relative to host tissue (Saiz-Lopez et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work

claim: RNA-seq was performed on pooled blocks of distal cells from HH24, HH24g, HH27 and HH29 chick wing buds

evidence: This describes the experimental procedure performed

claim: The region of undifferentiated mesenchyme is considered to extend proximally beneath the apical ectodermal ridge by 200 – 300 microns and to remain at a consistent length throughout outgrowth
source: The region of undifferentiated mesenchyme is considered to extend proximally beneath the apical ectodermal ridge by 200 – 300 microns and to remain at a consistent length throughout outgrowth (Summerbell et al., 1973)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work

claim: RNA was extracted from the distal 150 microns of control buds and grafts to ensure consistency between all samples
source: but for our analyses, we used RNA extracted from the distal 150 microns of control buds and grafts to ensure consistency between all samples.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure

claim: 55 genes are differentially expressed between the HH24g-HH24 pair

claim: 99 genes are differentially expressed between the HH24g-HH29 pair

source: There are five down-regulated pathways identified by the KEGG analyses in HH24g compared to HH29 distal cells - focal adhesion, ECM (extracellular matrix), gap junction, MAPK (Mitogen-Activated Protein Kinase) and actin cytoskeleton - suggesting a general reset of genes in these pathways that increase in expression over time between HH24 and HH29.

claim: The MAPK pathway is up-regulated in HH24g compared to HH29 distal cells

This divided the genes into three clusters (See Materials and methods – note three genes were excluded that fell into more than one cluster).

claim: Cluster 3 contains 53 genes that decrease in expression between HH24 and HH29 and are reset in HH24g grafts

claim: Genes in cluster one reflect stability of expression while genes in clusters 2 and 3 show reversibility of expression
